notes.meaning: David did not let his older brother's angry words stop him. He turned to another soldier and asked the same question until the news of his questions spread through the camp. God was quietly moving David's heart to step forward and speak up for Israel.

Soldiers heard David speaking with bold confidence and reported his words to King Saul. Saul then sent for the young shepherd to come to his tent. God often uses ordinary, humble people to bring courage to leaders and nations.

David told Saul that no one should lose heart because of Goliath. The young shepherd offered to go out and fight the giant himself. He did not ask about the king's riches or rewards, because his real aim was to defend God's honor.

Saul told David he was not able to fight the Philistine because he was only an inexperienced youth. Goliath, on the other hand, had been trained for war since his boyhood. Saul looked only at natural human strength instead of trusting in God's power.

David explained to Saul how he cared for his father's flock. Whenever a lion or a bear came to steal a lamb, David chased it, rescued the lamb, and struck the wild animal dead. His quiet years as a faithful shepherd had been God's training ground for this battle.

David declared that Goliath would end up just like the lion and the bear. The Philistine had insulted the armies of the living God, which made him an enemy of God Himself. David knew that no enemy can stand when fighting against the Lord.

David gave God all the credit for saving him from the lion and the bear, and he trusted God to save him from Goliath too. Saul was moved by David's strong faith and gave him permission to go with the Lord's blessing. Remembering how God has helped us in the past gives us courage for hard times today.

Saul dressed David in his own heavy battle tunic, bronze helmet, and coat of armor. The king meant well, but he was still thinking only in terms of human military weapons. God had a very different plan for how this victory would be won.

David strapped on the sword and tried to walk, but the heavy royal armor weighed him down. He told Saul he could not wear them because he was not used to such equipment. David took the armor off, choosing to trust God rather than human defenses.

David picked up his shepherd's staff, his leather sling, and five smooth stones from a dry riverbed. Smooth stones were chosen because they would fly straight and fast through the air. Going to battle with ordinary shepherd tools showed that the victory would belong to God alone.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine suggested that the five smooth stones represented the five books of Moses, from which Christ later drew Scripture to overcome the devil in the wilderness.

notes.meaning: Goliath marched forward toward David with a helper carrying a large shield in front of him. The giant carried heavy weapons in both hands and trusted completely in his armor and size. He approached with great pride, not knowing what God was about to do.

Goliath looked closely and felt insulted when he saw who had stepped out to meet him. David was only a young boy with bright, healthy looks rather than a tough soldier. The giant despised him because he judged David only by outward appearance.

Goliath asked if David thought he was just a dog, since David came at him with a wooden stick. He then cursed David using the names of his Philistine gods. The giant had no idea that the living God of heaven was standing with the young shepherd.

Goliath shouted that he would tear David apart and leave his body for wild birds and beasts to eat. Ancient warriors often yelled threats at each other before fighting to cause fear. Goliath trusted completely in his own strength, but his pride was leading him to ruin.

David answered that Goliath came with a sword, spear, and javelin, but David came in the name of the Lord of Hosts. This title means God rules over all the armies of heaven and earth. David stood firm because the giant had insulted the God of Israel.

David told Goliath that the Lord would hand him over that very day. He said he would strike the giant down, cut off his head, and defeat the Philistine army. David's goal was not personal fame, but that the entire world would learn that the true God lives in Israel.

David reminded the watching armies that the Lord does not need swords or spears to bring rescue. The fight belonged to God, and He would hand the Philistines over to Israel. When we face big problems, we can rest knowing that the battle belongs to the Lord.

As Goliath started moving forward to attack, David did not freeze or pull back. Instead, he ran quickly straight toward the battle line to meet the giant. David's faith made him bold because he was eager to defend God's name.

David reached into his pouch, took out a stone, and slung it with great force. God guided the stone straight to the giant's forehead, which was the only open spot not covered by armor. The stone sank deep into his skull, and Goliath fell flat on his face.

David conquered the giant with only a simple sling and a single stone. The story highlights that David did not even have a sword in his hand when Goliath was struck down. God proved that He can win the greatest victories through the humblest means.

David ran up, pulled Goliath's heavy sword from its sheath, and cut off the giant's head. When the Philistine army saw their greatest champion dead, panic spread and they all ran away. God used the enemy's own weapon to finish the victory.

The men of Israel and Judah shouted with joy and chased the fleeing Philistines all the way to Gath and Ekron. The road was littered with the bodies of the defeated enemy soldiers. God turned the army's long fear into a sweeping victory in a single hour.

After chasing the enemy, the Israelites returned to the abandoned Philistine camp and took all the plunder. They collected the valuable goods, food, and gear left behind by the fleeing army. God replaced His people's distress with great provision.

David brought Goliath's head toward Jerusalem as a sign of victory, and he kept the giant's weapons in his own tent. Goliath's sword was later dedicated to God in the sacred tabernacle. David honored the Lord by remembering who won the fight.

As Saul watched David walk out to face Goliath, he asked Abner the army commander whose son the young man was. Abner replied that he did not know. Saul needed to know David's family line because he had promised great tax freedom and royal rewards to the victor's household.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars point out that verses 55 through 58 are missing from early Greek copies of Samuel, suggesting they may have been added later to provide extra detail about David's family.

notes.meaning: Saul told Abner to go find out what family the brave young man came from. The king was eager to identify the household of someone who showed such astonishing courage. This inquiry soon led to David being brought permanently into royal service.

As soon as David returned from defeating Goliath, Abner brought him directly before King Saul. David was still carrying the head of the giant in his hand as proof of the victory. The young shepherd stood quietly before the king as God's chosen champion.

Saul asked David who his father was, and David humbly replied that he was the son of Jesse of Bethlehem. David did not brag about his great victory, but answered with quiet respect. God was now lifting up the faithful shepherd boy to a place of honor before the whole nation.
